Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
This article discusses resources and combinations in Jyhad. It discusses
the interplay of resources and combinations is so critical to operations
in Jyhad. It then lists some of the most common resources, and some good
ways to attack them. Finally, I close with some play tips based on my
theories.

In Jyhad you have a large and complex set of resources. I define a
resource as something you want and can use to do things but have a limited
supply of. The classic resources in Jyhad are pool, vampires, blood on
vampires, permanent assets (equipment, locations, etc.),and cards in your
hand. The complexity comes in that most of the resource categories must
be subdivided into smaller subcategories of resources. For example, if
you have a Malkavian/Ventrue vote deck, many of your Ventrue probably
won't have Obfuscate and accordingly won't help do things that require
vampires with Obfuscate. Likewise, blood on Thomas Thorne won't do you
any good if Lydia is in combat.

You accomplish things in Jyhad by stitching together the right particular
resources in combination to achieve results (costing your prey pool,
torporizing vampires, gaining pool, whatever). At the same time your
opponents are trying to do the same thing. To win, you need to make your
combinations keep working while your opponents' fail.

Why are combinations important? In many games (Magic for example) most
cards work OK alone, although they may be better in combination. Jyhad
differs. With a few exceptions, any card in Jyhad is worthless without at
least two or three companions. A + bleed card is junk if you don't have a
way to get it through. A combat card is junk if you can't get into
combat. A rush card is useless if you haven't any combat to back it up.
And just about everything needs a vampire who can use it.

The simplest basic combination in Jyhad is the Malkavian Stealthed bleed,
which requires an untapped vampire with Dominate and Obfuscate, a + bleed
card, and a stealth card. Often a second bleed card and several Obfuscate
cards are necessary as well. Other combinations are generally more
complex - Tremere intercept to 2nd round nuke will usually require at
least an untapped vampire with intercept and Thaumaturgy, and intercept
card, a press, and the 2nd round nuke. Often several additional combat
cards, of various types, are needed as well.

Now to make an action or a defense worthwhile, the whole combination must
work. Your predator will be throwing offensive combinations at you, while
your prey launches defenses. To survive (against your predator) or win
(against your prey) you must make their combinations fail. To succeed,
you need to find the link in their combination you can best attack and go
for it.

Why do you have to pick on one link? The reason is what I call the
2-for-1 rule. Two players (predator and prey) typically gun for your
throat. Now let's suppose your main interaction with predator and prey is
by combat (for simplicity). Every time you fight each side loses a couple
of blood. If everybody spent 20 bringing out vampires, by the time you've
lost 10 against your predator and 10 against your prey, you're down to 0
blood - and out of commission. Your opponents are still operational, at
10 each. Similar issues apply to other resources, like untapped vampires.

Your allies (grandpredator and grandprey) may help mess up your opponent
but they haven't much interest in your well-being per se. So you have to
be EFFICIENT - frying 2 resources for every one of yours, or CLEVER -
deactivating your opponent's entire tactic (thereby making all his
resources useless) by taking out only a few key resources. Relative
efficiency is hard to ensure - he may fight like a demon too - so
cleverness is at a premium. Because Jyhad operations demand combinations,
you can always be clever by picking on just one link of your opponent's
combinations.

Some of the classic resources, and ways to attack them.

Vampires with a particular skill - Combat is the way to go. Clan hosers,
Golconda and Hostile takeover can do nicely too. If he needs skill cards,
use your Sudden Reversals for them. This is a particularly important
resource for multi-clan decks, especially if the player relies on
disciplines not available to all the clans.

Untapped vampires - untap cards, combat-and-run-away, lots of vampires,
directed actions. This is a particularly important resource for decks
with large vampires.

Stealth abilities - intercept or rush. Intercept is better for light
stealth, rush for heavy stealth.

Bleed abilities - bleed bounce. Don't forget you may be able to attack
that which permits the bleed, like particular vampires, stealth, or combat
resources.

Equipment - intercept is the #1 method for this. Peace treaty is an
alternative for weapons. Drawing Out the Beast, Canine Horde, Blood
Rage/Fury, Fast Hands, and Shattering Blow work too. This tends to be
more important for decks with small vampires.

Intercept - stealth or combat abilities. Stealth is better for light
intercept, combat is better for heavy intercept. This tends to be
particularly important with newer players or with card limits (via fiat or
league).

Combat abilities - Dodge and maneuver are the first line of defense.
Fortitude works great too. If things are really hairy, avoid combat with
Combat Ends or with the Elysium.

Presses - Counter with your own presses, or Dodge the strikes your
opponent pressed to use. Again, Combat Ends is the trump.

I could go on and on with particular resources. Sometimes resources are
very specific, important to only a few decks, and the list would become
very long. But you can improve your play substantially by watching your
opponents and figuring out what their resources are. There's a lot of fun
in discovering the clever ways people have assembled resources, and
spotting the weak links for you to attack.

There was a design decision make with Jyhad on how to counter resources,
of almost any type. Generally a resource can be countered on a one-to-one
basis with a cheap card or tactic, or completely hosed with a more
difficult one. Bleed can be reduced with Telepathic Counter, or
redirected to benefit the original bleedee with Telepathic Misdirection or
Deflection. Maneuvers can be negated with Fake Out, or if there are too
many, you can use a gun instead. This is a very clever system, as it
maximizes defense flexibility. The flaw here is strike: combat ends,
which although clearly superior to dodges, presses, and maneuvers as
combat survival, costs no more and is not hard to get.

Permanent cards are an important part of flexibility. I believe that it's
a bad idea, generally, to rely on permanents as a basis of your strategy.
(Disguised/Concealed Weapon is a notable exception). Permanents are slow
to get out, and often vulnerable to intercept. However, permanents can
provide a boost for the circumstances where you need it. If you're
playing a Gangrel Claw deck against a mad maneuverer, a few guns are a big
help. If you don't need them, you have only a few cards to dispose of.
20 Form of the Ghost could catch the maneuverer too, but if you fight
somebody without maneuver, they'll jam your hand.

Somewhat surprisingly, the best resource to exhaust is often one of
particular cards. I call then the hand jam tactic. On the face of it,
this seems odd - typically a deck has a more-or-less unlimited supply of
any card it really needs. Hand jamming works because it doesn't matter
what's in your deck; what matters is what's in your hand when you need it.
In addition, normally you get more cards by playing the ones you have.
If you can't use anything in your hand, you're stuck - you can't get rid
of what's in your hand to get what you need from your library. You sit
there until you can discard enough to get going - or until you trick
somebody into exercising your hand.

Exercising a hand is the opposite of jamming it. A Malk S&B with bleed
bounce might have 1/4 Stealth, 1/4 Bleed, 1/4 bleed bounce, and 1/4
assorted Masters and Wakes. If you haven't got any intercept, attempting
to block him won't stop him - he'll just stealth on past, drawing more
bleed in the process. You've provided him "exercise" - the opportunity to
use parts of his deck that might have gone unused - and, as with people,
exercise makes decks healthier. If his predator bleeds, that's just
providing exercise too, because of the bleed bounce.

Deals with other players are an important part of attacking resources. To
jam your predator' or prey's hand, you almost always need at least
acquiescence, and usually the active assistance, of your grandpredator or
grandprey, respectively. Combat deck alliances are also particularly
lethal (provided there's some Rush involved), as non-combat decks usually
have good but limited anti-combat resources. Once they run out, vampires
go to go to torpor in a hurry.

What makes the interplay of combinations particularly difficult is that
the way you are attacking your opponents' combinations is generally- with
combinations of your own! So THEY, in turn, are busily trying to gum up
your ways to gum up their ways to gum up yours ways to ... well, you get
the idea. In addition, every combination you launch carries a cost in
resources - from slight (tapping a vampire or using some cards) to heavy
(hurling a sacrificial lamb like Dollface into the hands of Don Cruez to
prevent him from getting a Sports Bike). So everything you do has to be
based on an evaluation of long-term costs and benefits, taking into
account what the other players are doing. This interplay and constant
requirement for long-term thinking is what makes Jyhad such an intense,
involving, and interesting game.

So I sum up with a few tips:

Figure out your opponent's combinations, and plot out a strategy to attack
those combinations as soon as possible.

Figure out how your opponents will attack your combinations, and start
laying defenses.

Once you pick a target resource, stick to it. If you've been attacking a
Malk deck's vampires, and switch to attacking his stealth, your previous
work is largely wasted (unless, of course, you've been whaling on his
stealthy vampires). But if you must change, change as soon as possible so
you don't keep wasting effort.

Keep your long-term strategy in mind at all times.

Work in concert with your grandpredator and grandprey. But remember their
goals differ from yours - your grandprey wants to inactivate your prey's
offensive combinations while you want to get rid of your prey's defensive
ones.

Work to jam your opponent's hands and refrain from exercising them.

Happy Hunting.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

As a relatively new player of Jyhad, I found several of Curt Adams'
articles ("Strategies and Clans," "Jyhad Strategies," and his latest
article "Jyhad Tactics") all to be helpful. My wife and I do not yet have
access to a large group of players, so some strategic and tactical aspects
of the game have not yet become apparent to us.

For example, I am currently struggling with how to defeat a Mighty Gangrel
deck that my wife is playing against me. Curt's article has given me some
ideas on how to look for weaknesses in her deck. The important thing
about the article is not that it gave me mechanics (i.e., specific cards)
on how to attack her deck. Rather, it has given me ideas on methods to
attack her deck.

I acknowledge that such articles may not be of use to everyone who reads
this newsgroup, but these articles are useful to some of us. I am sure
many of the concepts that Curt Adams discusses have already been covered
in past newgroup ramblings. Nevertheless, the game (and this newsgroup)
will only thrive if we can attract new players and help them through the
somewhat confusing period of learning the game.

Thank you Curt for your efforts. Keep the good ideas and information
coming.

BilM...@aol.com
Bill Murray

Messages.Body:

I had a friend with a killer Gangrel deck that won many games (2 and
more players). My solution was Malkavians with weapons. I used
obfuscate to get past them for bleeding, dominate not only to bleed for
lots, but also to steal nasty allies & retainers (raven spy, gypsies,
renegade garou) and auspex to reduce bleeds and more importantly for
Fast Reactions to get them into a combat without them being able
to strike. Of course, a few Gangrel De-evolutions didn't hurt either.

Gary

Messages.Author: Owen Reynolds
Messages.Body:
>My only problem with the article was the portion on "making deals" I feel
>if you don't have the intelligence to create a winning deck then you
>shouldn't be trying to get people to do it for you.

>...I don't feel that this is the the type of game play that should be
>promoted.

That is one aspect of the game which is largely ignored and can
change the character of it immensely.
Way back when, my friends and I played multi-player Magic with the
"no table-talk" rule. You aren't allowed to make any explicit deals or
discuss anything at all about the contents of your hand. This makes
games go a lot faster, if anything else.

Other groups play all sort of multi-player games where you freely
discuss who you think is winning and what should be done about it, make
large deals, etc... . When you combine this with threats about what you'll
do if someone does what it looks like they might do, you get a lot of
talking between plays.

Jyhad politics, at least, encourages this sort of thing, almost
demands it. If I'm playing Parity Shift and can see votes on the table,
I've got to make a deal ahead of time before I say who gets how much
blood, so that the voters I need are happy.
KRCG pretty much says that you should stop and work out some kind of
deal before you spend a blood to give someone else's minion +1 intercept.
The bizzare victory conditions seem to encourage discussing who's
really winning, as well.

It's odd such a huge factor on game-play (some people practically
turn every game into Diplomacy) is almost completely ignored.

I figure if it's useful to them they'll read it and if it's not they
won't. I admit to enjoying compliments on what I write and to feeling
disappointed with myself when people find what i write a waste of time.
But that's just human nature; what people do with what I post is their
business.

>You may be thinking that I
>took the time in my demented life to read this, but you are wrong!! I
>glanced at it and decided that I HAD to respond.

Hmmm. Sounds like you had as much choice responding as I had writing.
Welcome to the club of the meme-infected :-)

>Find something better to do, maybe even play Jyhad.

Sometimes I wish I didn't play so much (1-3 nights a week, every week).
Fortunately/unfortunately I enjoy it immensely and it has become one of my
favorite recreational activities.

I do have something of an ulterior motive. I enjoy Jyhad immensely
because I find it really has something to sink your mental teeth (fangs?)
into. Yet not a lot of people play it, at least around here (there's only
2 substantial groups around here, to my knowledge). I often hear people
complain that they found certain styles to be winning styles, that they're
bored with the game, that the game is too slow and draggy. Yet the Jyhad
I know is very resistant to "superdecks", has incredible depth and
variety, and is better set up to satisfyingly develop and end than any
other multiplayer CCG I know. I hope that if somebody can put down in
writing what makes Jyhad such a great game, and how to have a great time
playing it, that will provide a tool to show people what a great game it
is and perhaps bring in more people. The more people play, the more fun I
will have.

I know there is a lot more the Jyhad than I understand and am (sometimes
painfully) aware of the deficiencies in my articles. If you see my pieces
as weak or only for beginners, write stronger ones, or ones better suited
to more advanced players. Even if nobody else would appreciate that, I
would - I love seeing well-thought-out pieces on Jyhad. IMO, if that's
fun (and believe me it is) and it helps other people, and it improves your
own play, it's well worth doing.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

Messages.Author: James C. Clover
Messages.Body:
> Jyhad politics, at least, encourages this sort of thing, almost
>demands it. If I'm playing Parity Shift and can see votes on the table,
>I've got to make a deal ahead of time before I say who gets how much
>blood, so that the voters I need are happy.
> KRCG pretty much says that you should stop and work out some kind of
>deal before you spend a blood to give someone else's minion +1 intercept.

I have to disagree with you here. When I play, I insist on a
no-kabitzing rule, ESPECIALLY when vote decks are afoot. If you pay
close attention to the text of these cards, you will notice that many, if
not most, of the vote cards create alliances simply by the nature of the
vote.

Let's take your example of Parity Shift. You distribute blood as you see
fit BEFORE the vote is called. If you have clear political superiority,
no problem, you give it all to yourself. If not, you have to distribute
some blood to other players who have votes on the table. The trick is
trying to figure out how little blood you can give away and still gain
enough support to win the vote. You also have to figure out who to try
to win support from. All these subtleties go away when you make verbal
deals.

Here's another example. Let's say somebody is kicking butt with a
location (maybe a combat deck with KRCG News Radio). You don't have the
votes to steal it with Disputed Territory. Disputed Territory says you
select a Methuselah to receive the location -- it's not automatically
you. So you select a player who won't benefit from it. You should win
the vote because only one player gets hurt, and nobody benefits. I think
this is a far more stimulating scenario than haggling for supporters.
Faster, too.

Then there are votes like Peace Treaty, Kindred Segregation,
Consanguineous Boon, Autarkis Persecution, and Kindred Restructure, which
probably benefit several players right off.

And then there's Cryptic Rider....
